raw_case_text:
A 63-year-old female with history of end stage renal disease secondary to IgA nephropathy, who underwent a living related kidney transplantation in 1995, presented to our hospital with generalized malaise, dyspnea on exertion, and cough which started 6 months prior. Her other past medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney allograft dysfunction due to recurrent IgA nephropathy. Immunosuppressive regimen included cyclosporine 100 mg every 12 hours, azathioprine 50 mg daily, and prednisone 5 mg daily. On arrival to the hospital, the patient was hypotensive with a blood pressure of 75/48 mmHg and febrile with a temperature of 100.6 F. Norepinephrine drip and broad-spectrum antibiotics were initiated, although a source of infection was not obvious at that time. Laboratory testing was notable for anemia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and C-reactive protein (CRP). CMV viral load was positive with a titer of 3.6 log10 IU/ml and valganciclovir therapy was initiated as a result. Morning cortisol level was substantially suppressed at 0.6mcg/dL, and, due to concern for adrenal insufficiency, stress dose hydrocortisone was administered, followed by conversion to prednisone taper. Patient's hypotension and fever resolved within 24 hours from the initial presentation, and she was subsequently discharged in stable condition with a diagnosis of CMV infection, on appropriate dose of valganciclovir with plan for follow-up as an outpatient. Unfortunately, the patient was rehospitalized 4 times in the subsequent 2 months with fever, shock, and fatigue. During each admission she received stress dose hydrocortisone and vasopressor with or without empiric antibiotics. Every time, her symptoms resolved rapidly (within 24 hours of initiation of therapy) without a clear diagnosis. Initially CMV was considered to be the cause of recurrent fever and hematologic abnormalities, but she had recurrent severe symptoms despite resolution of CMV viremia in the setting of valganciclovir treatment (summary in Table 1).
On the 5th admission, she presented again with hypotension and fever. The remainder of a review of symptoms was negative. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory testing revealed a white blood cell count of 7,200/mm3, persistent anemia with a hemoglobin of 8.2 g/dl, and thrombocytopenia with a platelet count of 83,000/mm3. LDH and CRP were yet again elevated (410 IU/L and 153.0 mg/L, respectively). Alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase were mildly elevated at 50 IU/L and 41 IU/L, respectively. The patient's serum triglyceride level was 547 mg/dl (normal range 0-149 mg/dl) and ferritin level was remarkably elevated at 3311 ng/ml (normal range 13-150 ng/ml). As outlined above, CMV viral load was undetectable. Vasopressor and stress dose hydrocortisone were administered. As patient's hypotension resolved, vasopressor was discontinued within 24 hours from the time of admission. A computed tomography scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed patchy ground glass opacities at the lung apices bilaterally. Bronchoscopy with broncho-alveolar lavage was performed, though it did not reveal any evidence of infection, including Pneumocystis jirovecii. Further testing was performed to exclude rheumatologic disease, macrophage activation syndrome, malignancy, and autoinflammatory syndromes. Complement levels were within normal limits; antinuclear antibodies and rheumatoid factor resulted as negative. Serum protein electrophoresis test showed normal levels of all immunoglobulins and no monoclonal component. EBV viral load was negative. Patient inevitably underwent a bone marrow biopsy, which revealed histiocytes with engulfed red cells, platelets, and neutrophils (Figure 1), suggesting HLH. High dose intravenous methylprednisolone was started at 1 gram intravenously daily and continued for 5 days, after which she was continued on oral prednisone at 1 mg/kg/day. Soluble Interleukin 2 receptor (sIL-2R) was elevated (15490 pg/ml, normal range <1033). Based on this, patient was diagnosed with HLH and discharged on high dose oral prednisone.
She remained afebrile, but suffered from severe persistent weakness. Subsequent outpatient laboratory testing revealed reduction of the platelet count and increased ferritin, indicating ongoing macrophage activation. Patient underwent thorough and extensive genetic testing, which was not consistent with familial HLH. Torso imaging was repeated to rule out an underlying malignancy, with positron emission tomography, and a magnetic resonance imaging did not reveal any suspicious neoplastic lesion. Given clinical and laboratory signs concerning for HLH exacerbation, chemotherapy with etoposide was started. She received four doses of etoposide in combination with daily dexamethasone. Unfortunately, patient developed acute hypoxic respiratory failure due to aspiration pneumonia in the setting of progressive encephalopathy, combined with Enterococcal and Neisseria bacteremia, and ultimately passed away within 3 months of her initial presentation.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 63-year-old female kidney transplant recipient presented with a 6-month history of generalized malaise, exertional dyspnea, and cough, accompanied by recurrent episodes of febrile hypotensive shock.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, who had undergone a living-related kidney transplant in 1995 for IgA nephropathy and was maintained on cyclosporine (100 mg q12h), azathioprine (50 mg daily), and prednisone (5 mg daily), presented with 6 months of malaise, exertional dyspnea, and cough, and arrived in febrile hypotensive shock (BP 75/48 mmHg, T 100.6 °F). Initial workup revealed anemia, thrombocytopenia, elevated LDH/CRP, suppressed morning cortisol (0.6 μg/dL), and CMV viremia (3.6 log10 IU/mL); she stabilized within 24 hours on norepinephrine, stress-dose hydrocortisone, and valganciclovir. Over the next 2 months, however, she required four additional readmissions for recurrent febrile shock and fatigue despite clearance of CMV viremia, culminating in a 5th admission for febrile shock and hematologic deterioration.
subjective.past_medical_history: End-stage renal disease secondary to IgA nephropathy status post living-related kidney transplantation in 1995; chronic kidney allograft dysfunction due to recurrent IgA nephropathy; type 2 diabetes mellitus; secondary adrenal insufficiency.
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial presentation positive for 6 months of generalized malaise, exertional dyspnea, cough, fever, and hypotension; 5th admission positive for recurrent fever, hypotension, and severe weakness. Home medications were cyclosporine (100 mg q12h), azathioprine (50 mg daily), prednisone (5 mg daily), and valganciclovir.

objective.physical_examination: Initial admission vital signs: Hypotensive with blood pressure 75/48 mmHg and febrile with temperature 100.6 °F. Fifth admission: Febrile and hypotensive with an otherwise unremarkable physical examination.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial admission labs: Anemia, thrombocytopenia, elevated LDH and CRP, suppressed morning serum cortisol (0.6 μg/dL), and positive plasma CMV viral load (3.6 log10 IU/mL). Fifth admission labs: WBC 7,200/mm3, hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL, platelets 83,000/mm3, LDH 410 IU/L, CRP 153.0 mg/L, ALT 50 IU/L, AST 41 IU/L, hypertriglyceridemia at 547 mg/dL (normal: 0–149 mg/dL), and marked hyperferritinemia at 3,311 ng/mL (normal: 13–150 ng/mL); undetectable plasma CMV and EBV viral loads; normal complement levels and serum protein electrophoresis; negative ANA and rheumatoid factor.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest, abdominal, and pelvic CT (5th admission): Patchy bilateral apical ground-glass opacities without lymphadenopathy or mass; subsequent whole-body PET and MRI negative for underlying malignancy. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Negative for all infectious agents, including Pneumocystis jirovecii. Bone marrow biopsy and HLH biomarkers: Demonstrated prominent hemophagocytosis (histiocytes engulfing erythrocytes, platelets, and neutrophils) and markedly elevated soluble IL-2 receptor (sIL-2R) at 15,490 pg/mL (normal <1,033 pg/mL); familial HLH genetic panel negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH; confirmed by bone marrow hemophagocytosis, sIL-2R 15,490 pg/mL, ferritin 3,311 ng/mL, triglycerides 547 mg/dL, bicytopenia, and recurrent febrile shock) initially triggered by cytomegalovirus (CMV) reactivation in a long-term renal transplant recipient, with Pneumocystis jirovecii and underlying lymphoma excluded by BAL and PET/MRI. Plan and clinical course: Treated on the 5th admission with pulse intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g/day for 5 days) followed by oral prednisone (1 mg/kg/day), and subsequently escalated for persistent outpatient macrophage activation to four doses of etoposide plus daily dexamethasone. Despite chemotherapy, she developed progressive encephalopathy, aspiration pneumonia with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, and Enterococcus and Neisseria bacteremia, and died within 3 months of initial presentation.
